subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement about atoms and elements is correct?
items.correct: Matter is made of atoms, and about 100 types of atom occur naturally.
items.misconception: Matter is made of atoms, and about 100 substances exist in total.
items.why: Students meet 'about 100 elements' as a striking fact and read it as a limit on substances rather than a limit on ingredients. The combinatorial step, that a small set of building blocks gives an unlimited set of products, is rarely made explicit. Treat the elements as an alphabet. Twenty-six letters give an unlimited number of words; about 100 types of atom give millions of compounds, because atoms can join in different numbers, ratios and arrangements.
items.random_wrong: Matter is made of atoms, and every element in the table is natural.

items.q: There are only about 100 naturally occurring types of atom, yet chemists have identified millions of different substances. How is this possible?
items.correct: Those atoms can join in many different ratios and arrangements.
items.misconception: Millions of other types of atom are still waiting to be discovered.
items.why: Students meet 'about 100 elements' as a striking fact and read it as a limit on substances rather than a limit on ingredients. The combinatorial step, that a small set of building blocks gives an unlimited set of products, is rarely made explicit. Treat the elements as an alphabet. Twenty-six letters give an unlimited number of words; about 100 types of atom give millions of compounds, because atoms can join in different numbers, ratios and arrangements.
items.random_wrong: Atoms change into atoms of new elements when substances react.

items.q: What does it mean to say that the elements show periodic relationships in their properties?
items.correct: Similar properties recur at regular intervals across the table.
items.misconception: Properties change smoothly from the first element to the last one.
items.why: Students are taught trends across a period and read them as a single global trend. The word 'periodic' is not connected to its everyday sense of happening again and again. Link 'periodic' to a repeating pattern, like the days of the week. Sodium behaves like lithium because the pattern has come round again, not because it is further along one line.
items.random_wrong: Only physical properties such as melting point follow a pattern.

items.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react vigorously with water in a similar way. Which feature of their atomic structure explains this?
items.correct: Each atom has just one electron in its outer shell.
items.misconception: Their atoms all contain the same total number of electrons.
items.why: Students know electrons explain the similarity but reach for the total count, which is the number they have practised writing. That the totals differ here is not noticed. Write the electronic structures: Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1. The totals differ, but each ends in 1. It is the outer shell that governs chemical behaviour.
items.random_wrong: Their atoms all have the same number of occupied shells.

items.q: According to the key ideas, in what ways can atoms bond to one another?
items.correct: By transferring electrons from one atom to another, or by sharing them.
items.misconception: By sharing electrons, or by fusing the two nuclei firmly together.
items.why: The everyday picture of things being glued together suggests the whole particles must join. Ball-and-stick models show two balls touching a rod, which looks like direct contact. In a covalent bond the shared electrons are attracted to both nuclei, holding the atoms a set distance apart. Joining nuclei would be a nuclear reaction, not a chemical one.
items.random_wrong: By transferring protons between atoms, or by sharing protons.

items.q: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide, MgO. What happens to electrons as this compound forms?
items.correct: Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to an oxygen atom.
items.misconception: Each magnesium atom shares its two electrons with an oxygen atom.
items.why: Sharing is taught first and feels like the friendly, general case. Students then apply it everywhere instead of asking which types of element are involved. Metal with non-metal means transfer and ions; non-metal with non-metal means sharing and molecules. Magnesium oxide contains Mg2+ and O2-, not shared pairs.
items.random_wrong: Each oxygen atom transfers two electrons to a magnesium atom.

items.q: Why do the key ideas say that the shapes of molecules and the arrangement of giant structures are of great importance?
items.correct: Because how the particles are arranged decides how they behave.
items.misconception: Because the shape of a substance decides only how it looks to us.
items.why: Composition is the first thing students learn to read from a formula, so it becomes the whole explanation. Structure is treated as a picture rather than as a cause. Diamond and graphite both contain only carbon atoms, yet one is the hardest natural substance and the other is soft and conducts. The arrangement is the difference.
items.random_wrong: Because two substances made of the same atoms always behave alike.

items.q: Diamond and graphite are both giant structures containing only carbon atoms, yet graphite is soft and conducts electricity while diamond is hard and does not. Why?
items.correct: The carbon atoms are bonded in different arrangements.
items.misconception: Graphite holds a small amount of metal that carries the current.
items.why: Every conductor students handle, from wires to coins, is metallic, so conduction and metal become one idea. Conduction needs charged particles that are free to move. In graphite the delocalised electrons between the layers do that job, and graphite contains only carbon.
items.random_wrong: Graphite contains a softer type of carbon atom than diamond does.

items.q: The key ideas state that there are barriers to reaction. What does this mean?
items.correct: Colliding particles need a minimum amount of energy before they react.
items.misconception: Reacting particles are kept apart by a physical layer between them.
items.why: The word barrier is concrete in everyday use. The oxide layer on magnesium ribbon is also called a barrier, which reinforces the physical reading. The barrier is a minimum energy, not an object. Even when particles are thoroughly mixed and colliding constantly, most collisions fail because they are not energetic enough.
items.random_wrong: Substances have to be melted before their particles can react.

items.q: Two different reactions are carried out at the same temperature and concentration, but one goes much more slowly than the other. What best explains the difference?
items.correct: The slower reaction has the higher energy barrier to overcome.
items.misconception: A physical barrier keeps its particles apart in the flask.
items.why: The word barrier is concrete in everyday use. The oxide layer on magnesium ribbon is also called a barrier, which reinforces the physical reading. The barrier is a minimum energy, not an object. Even when particles are thoroughly mixed and colliding constantly, most collisions fail because they are not energetic enough.
items.random_wrong: The slower reaction releases less energy overall than the faster.

items.q: The key ideas state that chemical reactions take place in only three different ways. What are those three ways?
items.correct: Proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing.
items.misconception: Proton transfer, neutron transfer and electron transfer only.
items.why: Protons, neutrons and electrons are learnt as one list of three, so students assume all three are equally available to take part in reactions. Neutrons are locked in the nucleus and move only in nuclear changes. The specification names exactly three ways: proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing.
items.random_wrong: Proton sharing, neutron sharing and electron transfer only.

items.q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide solution. In terms of the three ways reactions take place, what happens here?
items.correct: A proton is transferred from the acid to the alkali.
items.misconception: An electron is transferred from the acid to the hydroxide ions.
items.why: Electron transfer is the transfer students practise most, in redox and in ionic bonding, so it becomes the default answer whenever something is transferred. Acids supply H+ ions, and an H+ ion is simply a proton. Neutralisation is H+ + OH- giving H2O, which is proton transfer, not electron transfer.
items.random_wrong: A proton is transferred from the alkali across to the acid.

items.q: A strip of zinc is placed in copper sulfate solution. The blue colour fades and copper is deposited on the zinc. Which of the three ways of reacting is this?
items.correct: Electron transfer, because zinc atoms lose electrons to copper ions.
items.misconception: Electron sharing, because zinc and copper share electrons here.
items.why: Sharing is taught first and feels like the friendly, general case. Students then apply it everywhere instead of asking which types of element are involved. Metal with non-metal means transfer and ions; non-metal with non-metal means sharing and molecules. Magnesium oxide contains Mg2+ and O2-, not shared pairs.
items.random_wrong: Proton transfer, because zinc gives protons to copper ions.

items.q: Which of these changes is an example of electron sharing?
items.correct: Two hydrogen atoms bond together to form a hydrogen molecule.
items.misconception: Sodium and chlorine atoms react to form solid sodium chloride.
items.why: Sharing is taught first and feels like the friendly, general case. Students then apply it everywhere instead of asking which types of element are involved. Metal with non-metal means transfer and ions; non-metal with non-metal means sharing and molecules. Magnesium oxide contains Mg2+ and O2-, not shared pairs.
items.random_wrong: A magnesium atom loses two electrons and becomes an ion.

items.q: What does it mean to say that energy is conserved in chemical reactions?
items.correct: Energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transferred.
items.misconception: Reactions that give out heat create the energy that they release.
items.why: Energy appears as warmth where there was none before, so making it seems the natural description, and 'gives out energy' sounds like production. Energy is neither created nor destroyed. The energy released was already in the chemical store of the reactants; the reaction only moves it to the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: Energy is gradually used up, which is why reactions stop.

items.q: During a reaction in an open beaker, the mixture and the beaker both become noticeably hotter. What has happened to the energy?
items.correct: It has all been transferred out to the surroundings.
items.misconception: The reaction has created new energy as the products formed.
items.why: Energy appears as warmth where there was none before, so making it seems the natural description, and 'gives out energy' sounds like production. Energy is neither created nor destroyed. The energy released was already in the chemical store of the reactants; the reaction only moves it to the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: Some of the energy was destroyed as the new bonds formed.

items.q: Does every element shown in the periodic table occur naturally?
items.correct: No. About 100 types of atom occur naturally; the remaining elements in the table have been made artificially in nuclear reactions.
items.misconception: Every element printed in the periodic table is one of the naturally occurring types of atom.
items.why: The periodic table is presented as one finished, authoritative object, so students assume nature supplies every box in it. The distinction between naturally occurring and synthetic elements is rarely drawn. Count the boxes in a full periodic table: there are more than 100. The specification says 'about 100 naturally occurring' precisely because the heaviest elements were made in laboratories, not found in rocks.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does water contain a special 'water atom'?
items.correct: No. Water contains hydrogen atoms and oxygen atoms bonded together. There is no separate type of atom for each compound.
items.misconception: Each different compound must contain its own unique type of atom.
items.why: Students carry over the everyday idea that a new material needs a new ingredient. Particle diagrams that draw a compound as a single blob reinforce it. A compound is built from atoms of the elements it contains. Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. No new type of atom appears.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do atoms turn into atoms of a different element during a chemical reaction?
items.correct: No. Chemical reactions rearrange atoms and move electrons or protons; the atoms themselves are not changed into other elements.
items.misconception: New elements are made during chemical reactions, and that is where new substances come from.
items.why: Products often look nothing like the reactants, so students conclude the atoms themselves must have changed. Nuclear reactions met in physics lessons blur the boundary further. Check any balanced equation: the same atoms appear on both sides, only joined up differently. Changing one element into another needs a nuclear change, not a chemical one.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which elements have similar chemical properties: those in the same period or the same group?
items.correct: Those in the same group, because their atoms have the same number of electrons in the outer shell.
items.misconception: Elements in the same period have similar properties, because the pattern is called 'periodic'.
items.why: The word 'periodic' sounds as though it points to the periods. Rows and columns are also easily swapped when students read the table at speed. Periods are the rows; groups are the columns. Similar properties run down the columns. Sodium and potassium are both in Group 1 and both react vigorously with water.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do periodic patterns apply to physical properties only?
items.correct: No. Chemical properties such as reactivity and physical properties such as melting point both show periodic relationships.
items.misconception: Only measurable physical properties such as melting point follow the periodic pattern.
items.why: Physical properties are the ones plotted on graphs, so they are the ones students see patterned. Chemical reactivity is taught separately as group chemistry. Group 1 reactivity increasing down the group and Group 7 reactivity decreasing down the group are chemical patterns. The specification names both chemical and physical properties.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do elements whose atoms have the same number of occupied shells behave alike?
items.correct: No. Atoms with the same number of occupied shells are in the same period, and their properties differ across that period.
items.misconception: Similar chemical behaviour comes from having the same number of electron shells.
items.why: Shells are the most visible feature of an atom diagram, so students use shell count as the point of comparison instead of outer-shell electron count. Sodium and chlorine both have three occupied shells, yet one is a reactive metal and the other a reactive non-metal. Compare the outer shells, not the number of shells.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which particles are moved or shared when atoms bond?
items.correct: Electrons. Atoms bond by transferring electrons from one atom to another or by sharing electrons.
items.misconception: Atoms bond by transferring or sharing protons.
items.why: Proton transfer is met as one of the three ways reactions happen, so students blur it with bonding. Protons and electrons are also easily confused as 'the charged bits'. Protons sit in the nucleus and stay there during bonding. Only outer electrons are transferred or shared when atoms bond to one another.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In magnesium oxide, which atom loses the electrons?
items.correct: The magnesium atom loses two electrons to the oxygen atom, forming Mg2+ and O2-.
items.misconception: The oxygen atom gives its electrons to the magnesium atom.
items.why: Oxygen is described as the reactive, attacking element, so students assume it is the one doing the giving. The direction of transfer is often left unstated. Metals lose electrons; non-metals gain them. Magnesium has two outer electrons to lose, and oxygen needs two to fill its outer shell, giving MgO.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a giant structure just a very large molecule?
items.correct: No. A molecule is a fixed small group of bonded atoms; a giant structure is a continuous repeating lattice with no set number of atoms.
items.misconception: Giant covalent substances such as diamond are simply enormous molecules with a formula like any other.
items.why: Both are drawn as balls joined by sticks, and both involve covalent bonds, so the only apparent difference is size. Water is always H2O, three atoms. A diamond crystal has no set number of carbon atoms; the lattice just repeats, which is why melting it means breaking bonds throughout.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does every collision between reactant particles cause a reaction?
items.correct: No. Only collisions with at least the minimum energy, and in a suitable direction, lead to a reaction.
items.misconception: Particles react every time they collide, so the rate depends only on how often they collide.
items.why: Collision theory is introduced through 'more collisions means faster', and the energy condition is dropped when students summarise it. Hydrogen and oxygen collide billions of times a second at room temperature yet barely react. A spark supplies the energy that gets collisions over the barrier.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a fast reaction always release more energy than a slow one?
items.correct: No. Rate and energy change are separate ideas. A slow reaction can release far more energy in total than a fast one.
items.misconception: The faster a reaction goes, the more energy it must give out overall.
items.why: Vigorous reactions look and sound energetic, so speed and energy are fused into a single idea of being powerful. Rusting is extremely slow but releases a large amount of energy overall. Rate depends on the size of the barrier; energy change depends on reactants and products.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In an acid and alkali reaction, which way does the proton move?
items.correct: From the acid to the alkali. The acid donates the hydrogen ion and the alkali accepts it.
items.misconception: The alkali donates a proton to the acid.
items.why: Alkalis are described as the strong or aggressive partner in neutralisation, so students assume the alkali is the one giving something away. Acids are proton donors; bases and alkalis are proton acceptors. HCl gives its H+ to the OH- from sodium hydroxide, and water is formed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is neutralisation just the mixing and diluting of two solutions?
items.correct: No. A new substance, water, is formed and energy is released, so a chemical reaction has taken place.
items.misconception: Adding an alkali to an acid simply dilutes the acid until it is no longer acidic.
items.why: Both liquids look the same before and after, and adding water really does raise the pH of an acid, so dilution seems a sufficient explanation. The mixture warms up and a salt can be crystallised from it. Dilution on its own never produces heat or a new solid product.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is energy used up and lost in a chemical reaction?
items.correct: No. Energy is conserved. It is transferred between the chemicals and the surroundings, never destroyed.
items.misconception: Some energy is destroyed or used up during a reaction, which is why reactions eventually stop.
items.why: Everyday language talks of using up the energy in a battery or a fuel. Energy that has spread out into the surroundings is no longer useful, which students read as gone. Track where the energy went. When a fuel burns, energy stored in the chemicals has been transferred to the surroundings, which are now warmer. The total is unchanged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.11 Key ideas
